question: How is إبراهيم read and syntactically governed?

positions.position: In the common accusative reading, it is coordinated with Noah: God also sent Abraham.
positions.reasons: Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās and al-Kisāʾī supply 'We sent' from 29:14. Al-Kashshāf and al-Nasafī connect it with Abraham's readiness to counsel. Al-Biqāʿī prefers this construction by the later Midian parallel; al-Ālūsī prefers it by 29:36. Al-Rāzī and al-Samīn identify the accusative as common. Al-Bursawī adds an implied command to recall the time of speech.

positions.position: In the accusative, an omitted 'Remember' governs Abraham.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī makes 'when he said' an inclusion apposition since the time contains the event. Al-Biqāʿī says recalling the exemplary forefather comforts the Prophet and instructs his people. Al-Ālūsī permits coordination of stories with different forms.

positions.position: In the nominative reading, an omitted predicate gives 'Among the messengers was Abraham.'
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf names al-Nakhaʿī and Abū Ḥanīfa as readers; Abū Ḥayyān adds Abū Jaʿfar and Ibrāhīm. Al-Samīn makes Abraham the subject. Al-Ālūsī favors this supplied predicate in light of 29:14–15.

positions.position: The accusative Abraham is coordinated with the object pronoun of 'We saved him' in 29:15.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Kisāʾī and al-Samīn allow it. Al-Ālūsī reports Abū al-Baqāʾ and Ibn ʿAṭiyya offering it, but calls it poor.

positions.position: The nominative may instead supply 'among those to be mentioned' or 'among those saved.'
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports both estimates and prefers 'among the messengers' because of the surrounding verses.

turns_on: The case reading and, for the accusative, the governing verb; the surrounding sending formula supports the preferred coordination.

question: What is the grammatical function of إذ قال?

positions.position: It marks the time of God's sending Abraham.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf says he could then counsel through age and knowledge; al-Bayḍāwī says judgment and recognition of truth had matured; al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī say he was ready to exhort and guide.

positions.position: It is an inclusion apposition to Abraham under an omitted 'Remember.'
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī says the time contains the event; al-Samīn and al-Biqāʿī give the same parse. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī allow it with omitted 'remember.' Abū Ḥayyān objects that past-time idh is not a direct object, and al-Ālūsī reports his objection to making its indeclinable temporal form an object or substitution.

positions.position: An implied command asks the audience to remember the time of his speech.
positions.reasons: Al-Bursawī combines coordination of Abraham with Noah and this implicit recollection.

turns_on: Whether idh modifies sending or belongs to an omitted 'remember'; Abū Ḥayyān disputes the appositional object analysis.

question: When was Abraham sent in relation to his call?

positions.position: He was sent when mature enough in age, judgment and knowledge to counsel his people.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī make this the sense of the temporal phrase.

positions.position: He remained a messenger while speaking; sending is a continuing state.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī raises the problem that preaching ordinarily follows sending and compares ongoing messengerhood to standing that lasts until a prince exits his house.

positions.position: He began calling people through divine guidance before formal sending, which happened while he preached.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī offers this as another resolution of the order problem. Al-Ālūsī reports a similar proposal near adulthood but replies that Abraham's words at 29:18, if his, suggest prior sending; al-Saʿdiyya says the verse need not imply formal mission.

turns_on: Whether 'when he said' requires sending to coincide with speech, and whether 29:18 attests an already existing mission.

question: How does Abraham's account connect with Noah's and Quraysh?

positions.position: It continues Noah's account by introducing another prophet God sent.
positions.reasons: Yaḥyā ibn Sallām links it to 29:14; al-Zajjāj supplies the sending verb. Al-Biqāʿī cites the later Midian parallel, and al-Ālūsī joins the stories despite differing sentence forms.

positions.position: It offers Quraysh a parallel and recalls their forefather's rejection of idols.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān make the analogy explicit. Al-Biqāʿī says remembering Abraham comforts the Prophet and instructs his people.

question: Who were Abraham's people in this account?

positions.position: His own people, identified as Nimrod and the idolaters of his city in Babylon.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān mention Nimrod and his idol-worshiping city; al-Bursawī names Babylon and includes Nimrod. Al-Biqāʿī stresses Abraham addressed his own people.

question: What is reported about Abraham before he called his people?

positions.position: He grew unusually fast, then went out to call his people.
positions.reasons: Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports al-Suddī: each day of growth equaled a week and each week a month.

question: What does اعبدوا الله ask Abraham's people to do?

positions.position: Worship God alone, affirming His oneness instead of idols or intermediaries.
positions.reasons: Muqātil and Yaḥyā gloss worship as oneness; Ibn ʿAṭiyya sets the call among Nimrod's idolaters. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says exclusivity is implicit: idolaters worship angels and jinn as intermediaries to God. Kur'an Yolu asks whether idols have divine qualities. Al-Rāzī argues possible beings require a necessary existent, and two necessary beings would be composite through shared and distinguishing attributes; no partner can share God's status. Ibn Kathīr adds sincere worship, provision sought only from God, and thanks to the sole giver.

positions.position: Obey God by performing His worship and obligations.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās says 'obey'; al-Ṭabarī says to discharge duties. Al-Rāzī includes affirmation of God and rejection of shirk within obligations and prohibitions. Al-Biqāʿī says worship as God directs. Study Quran calls it a summary of appeals in 19:42, 19:48, 21:52, 21:66, 26:69, 26:76, 37:85 and 37:95.

positions.position: Affirm God's existence.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī reports a paired reading: worship affirms God, while piety denies other gods; association with the sovereign is a grave offense.

turns_on: The command is unpacked as exclusive monotheism, practical obedience or affirmation of God's existence; al-Rāzī explicitly gives alternative readings.

question: What does وَٱتَّقُوهُ ask them to do?

positions.position: Fear God and His punishment.
positions.reasons: Al-Suddī, Muqātil and Ibn ʿAbbās say fear God. Al-Qurṭubī specifies His punishment and torment; al-Biqāʿī links association with punishment. Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran speak of reverence alongside worship.

positions.position: Avoid sins and prohibited acts.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī says to avoid sins while performing duties; al-Rāzī pairs obligations with abstention from prohibitions.

positions.position: Avoid associating anything with God.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī says piety denies any other deity because a partner with the sovereign is a grave offense. Al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī explicitly link fear to shunning shirk; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the pair a summons to monotheism and a warning.

turns_on: The explanations specify fear itself, abstention from forbidden deeds, or especially avoidance of shirk.

question: With what is ذَٰلِكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ compared?

positions.position: Worship and piety are better than their idolatry, unbelief or current practice.
positions.reasons: Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bursawī contrast idols or unbelief; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī name current practice. Al-Bursawī says the comparative accommodates their false belief, though unbelief contains no good. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr glosses khayr as afḍal, 'better or more excellent.' Al-Jishumī and al-Baghawī state the advantage generally; Ibn Kathīr says it earns good and averts evil.

positions.position: Worship and reverent fear are better than everything beneficial.
positions.reasons: Al-Biqāʿī says better than anything; al-Ālūsī reports comparison with all beneficial things.

positions.position: Khayr can mean simply 'good,' without comparison.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports this alternative alongside both comparative construals.

turns_on: Whether khayr compares worship with idolatry, all goods, or nothing.

question: Why are worship and piety better for people?

positions.position: They bring benefit and avert harm in this life and the hereafter.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathīr says worship, fear, seeking provision from God and thanking the giver bring good and repel evil in both lives. Kur'an Yolu says obedience benefits people; disbelief harms worldly life and prevents salvation in the hereafter.

positions.position: They draw a person near to sovereign God and raise that person's rank.
positions.reasons: Al-Rāzī argues humans cannot own heaven and earth, so their highest rank is nearness to the sovereign. He cites 96:19 on prostration and two divine sayings about drawing near through obligations and continued worship. An atheist denies the sovereign, while an idolater posits inferior partners; uniqueness, worship and piety yield higher status to one who understands the proofs.

positions.position: Serving God protects human dignity and personality.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu says serving others damages these, whereas worship and obedience to God benefit the worshiper.

question: What does إِن كُنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ require or imply?

positions.position: They must discern benefit from harm and good from evil with reasoned insight.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī invokes recognizing good and harm, with 6:72 and 9:41. Al-Zamakhsharī contrasts discernment with blind ignorance; al-Bayḍāwī contrasts knowledge with ignorance. Al-Ālūsī says even any knowledge suffices to recognize the advantage. Al-Jishumī and al-Bursawī speak of understanding and discernment.

positions.position: They must know God is their Lord.
positions.reasons: Al-Wāḥidī reports al-Kalbī's gloss.

positions.position: The condition rebukes their actual ignorance.
positions.reasons: Muqātil says they do not know; Ibn al-Jawzī says they fail to know good from bad. Al-Biqāʿī argues even animals seek their benefit, so people who miss this are below animals despite claims to reason.

turns_on: Whether the condition specifies practical discernment, recognition of God as Lord, or censures their ignorance.

question: Whose speech is the following passage?

positions.position: The verses continue Abraham's speech.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf reports this for the passage through the endpoint it names as 27:56.

positions.position: The verses include an aside about Muhammad and Quraysh within Abraham's story.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf reports this alternative for the same passage.

turns_on: Whether the discourse remains Abraham's or interrupts it with an aside.

question: How does this call relate to other Qur'anic portrayals of Abraham and prophetic faith?

positions.position: Islam renews Abraham's creed, which believers are told to follow.
positions.reasons: Study Quran says the Qur'an treats Abraham in over two hundred verses and cites 6:161, 2:130, 3:95, 16:123, 2:135 and 3:67 for following and defining faith by his creed.

positions.position: This command summarizes Abraham's longer appeals elsewhere.
Calling people to the one God is a principle shared by all prophets.
positions.reasons: Kur'an Yolu connects it with examining idols' supposed divinity and remembering earlier peoples who called messengers liars.
